library: Hillsborough has no commercial or civic center of its own; the nearest library is in Burlingame
middle: Public · 6–8, Hillsborough City School District, opened 1959
high: San Mateo Union High School District
Public · 9–12 — Hillsborough has no high school; students attend Burlingame High or another district campus

carolands.intro: Carolands takes its name from the 98-room chateau Harriett Pullman Carolan completed in 1916, and the estate’s 554 acres are the reason the neighborhood exists — they were subdivided through the 1940s and 1950s as the great Hillsborough houses became impossible to staff. The chateau itself survived, restored by Charles and Ann Johnson in 1998, and the Carolands Foundation now runs free docent tours by lottery.
amenities: The 1916 Pullman house at the center of the neighborhood, open for docent tours
Hillsborough has no shops; groceries are in Burlingame
The nearest restaurants and cafes, down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

tobin-clark-estate.intro: The Tobin Clark Estate is named for the Cotswold-style house Tobin Clark built in 1931, known locally as the House-on-Hill, which is still a private residence rather than a school or a museum — unusual among Hillsborough’s surviving great houses. The neighborhood around it was subdivided from the estate grounds and keeps their scale.
amenities: The private club, founded 1893 and the first west of the Mississippi
Hillsborough has no commercial zoning; groceries are down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District, built 1917

skyfarm.intro: Skyfarm began as a wedding gift from William H. Crocker to his sister-in-law, and the house eventually became the centerpiece of the Nueva School — one of two Hillsborough estates that survived by turning into a campus. The neighborhood took shape on the land around it after the war, on the half-acre minimum lots the town has required since incorporation.
amenities: The former Skyfarm estate, now a school campus at the neighborhood’s heart
Restaurants and shops down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

brewer-subdivision.intro: The Brewer subdivision sits alongside the Uplands estate, which outlasted the era by becoming Crystal Springs Uplands School rather than being demolished. Like most of Hillsborough, the housing here came from breaking up estate land after the Second World War, and the streets still follow the contours the original grounds were laid out on.
amenities: The former Uplands estate, adjoining the neighborhood
Hillsborough has no shops of its own
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

country-club-manor.intro: Country Club Manor sits near the Burlingame Country Club, whose founding in 1893 was the reason the first buyers came to these hills at all. Houses here are among the newer and larger in Hillsborough, set in heavy tree cover, and they come to market rarely enough that a single sale can reset expectations for the street.
amenities: The private club that started Hillsborough, founded 1893
Groceries down the hill; the town has no commercial zoning
Restaurants and shops nearby in Burlingame
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

hillsborough-park.intro: Hillsborough Park lies in the older, lower part of town nearest Burlingame, where the earliest subdivisions went in and where the eucalyptus John McLaren planted in the 1850s still shapes the streets. Lots meet the town’s half-acre minimum and, as everywhere in Hillsborough, there are no sidewalks — a rule written into the town at incorporation in 1910.
amenities: The private club adjoining the older part of town
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

hillsborough-heights.intro: Hillsborough Heights climbs the middle of the town, on land broken out of the estates after the war. The half-acre minimum and the absence of sidewalks give it the same character as the rest of Hillsborough — houses set well back behind mature planting, and streets that carry almost nothing but residents.
amenities: The private club below the neighborhood
Hillsborough has no shops; groceries are in Burlingame
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

hillsborough-hills.intro: Hillsborough Hills occupies the higher western ground, where the terrain is steepest and the parcels largest. It is among the quietest corners of a town that has no commerce at all, and the combination of elevation and tree cover means many houses are effectively invisible from the road.
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

hillsborough-knolls.intro: Hillsborough Knolls is one of the smaller pockets in a town of about eleven thousand people, on rolling ground subdivided from estate land in the postwar decades. Turnover is low even by Hillsborough standards — a handful of houses change hands in a typical year.
amenities: The private club, a short drive
The nearest grocery, down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

hillsborough-oaks.intro: Named for the oaks that predate every house on it, Hillsborough Oaks is a wooded pocket on the town’s western side. The planting here is old enough that the neighborhood reads as woodland with houses in it rather than the other way round, which is close to what the town has always been aiming for.
amenities: Hillsborough has no commercial zoning of its own
The nearest dining, down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

homeplace.intro: Homeplace is one of the fourteen designated neighborhoods the town recognizes, on ground subdivided from the estates in the middle of the last century. It has what the whole of Hillsborough has — half-acre lots, no sidewalks, no shops — and, like its neighbors, a market measured in a handful of sales a year rather than a month.
amenities: The private club, a short drive away
Restaurants and shops down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

lakeview.intro: Lakeview sits on the western side of Hillsborough toward the Crystal Springs watershed, and its position is the appeal — the reservoir land beyond means nothing will ever be built on that horizon. Houses are large and set on the town’s customary half-acre minimum, in heavy tree cover.
amenities: Protected reservoir land forming the town’s western horizon
The nearest grocery, down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

parrot-drive-area.intro: The Parrott Drive area takes its name from the estate family whose land it was, and it runs through some of the more secluded ground in the town. Even by Hillsborough standards the houses here sit far back from the road behind gates and tree rows, which is precisely what the town’s founding rules were written to produce.
amenities: Protected open land on the western horizon
Hillsborough has no shops of its own
The nearest restaurants, down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

ryan-tract.intro: The Ryan Tract is one of the postwar subdivisions carved out of estate land, and like most of them it kept the mature planting that came with the ground. It is a small neighborhood in a small town — Hillsborough has no commercial district, no sidewalks and about eleven thousand residents — and it trades accordingly, a few houses at a time.
amenities: The private club, a short drive
Restaurants and shops down the hill
schools: Public · K–5, Hillsborough City School District

burlingame-hills.intro: Burlingame Hills is not part of Hillsborough or of Burlingame — it is unincorporated San Mateo County, wedged between the two, which means county services rather than city ones and a different set of rules from either neighbor. The housing is hillside and mid-century, and the position, minutes from Burlingame Avenue and the freeway, is what draws people to it.
amenities: Wooded canyon trails on the Burlingame side
Groceries a short drive down the hill
The restaurant and shopping street, close by
